## Guided Tutorial 12.3: Testing the Hours Behind the Variance

**Context and objective.** The committee wants to know whether the extra hours behind the manufacturing variance were worked, approved, recorded against the right operations, and paid correctly, and why so little indirect time appears in the records for four months of 2024. In this tutorial, you will profile the time records, reconcile the hours along the chain from the time clock to the payroll, test whose time was paid, and compare the pay with an expectation built from the hours and the pay rates. You will then test the overtime approvals and the days on which everyone clocked the same hours, test when direct time was recorded, and decide what the results mean for the variance.

**Prerequisites.** Complete Tutorials 12.1 and 12.2, and continue at the end of Audit.sql. If you start here, make the working copy as Step 1 of Tutorial 9.1 describes, and download Audit.sql as it stands at the end of Tutorial 12.2 from [Companion Files](#sec-companion-files). @fig-10-08 shows the payroll and time tables, and @fig-12-07 the chain of records that the tests follow.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Profile the time records.** Before testing the time clock entries, find out what they hold, with the tests of @tbl-10-03.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H1: a profile of the time clock entries
   -- Population: all clock entries; expected: approved and complete
   SELECT COUNT(*) AS Entries,
       SUM(CASE WHEN ClockStatus <> 'Approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           AS NotApproved,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(ClockOutTime) AS NoClockOut,
       COUNT(DISTINCT EmployeeID) AS Employees,
       MIN(WorkDate) AS FirstWorkDate, MAX(WorkDate) AS LastWorkDate
   FROM TimeClockEntry;
   ```

b. Read each column of the result.

The table holds tens of thousands of entries by several dozen employees, from 1 January 2024 to 11 December 2026, the last day with time records that Tutorial 10.3 found. A handful of entries are still waiting for approval, and three have no clock-out time; Steps 4 and 6 find whose they are. The profile also fixes the dates over which every total of this tutorial is measured.

**Step 2. Reconcile the hours along the chain.** Every hour clocked should be recorded as labor time and paid. Read the test from the top: the CTEs Clocked, Recorded, and Paid each total the hours of every pay period on one record, and the final query joins them on the period and counts the periods in which they differ.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H2: clocked, recorded, and paid hours
   -- Population: every pay period; expected: equal in every period
   WITH Clocked AS (
       SELECT PayrollPeriodID, SUM(RegularHours + OvertimeHours) AS Hours
       FROM TimeClockEntry
       GROUP BY PayrollPeriodID
   ),
   Recorded AS (
       SELECT PayrollPeriodID, SUM(RegularHours + OvertimeHours) AS Hours
       FROM LaborTimeEntry
       GROUP BY PayrollPeriodID
   ),
   Paid AS (
       SELECT pr.PayrollPeriodID, SUM(prl.Hours) AS Hours
       FROM PayrollRegisterLine AS prl
           INNER JOIN PayrollRegister AS pr
               ON pr.PayrollRegisterID = prl.PayrollRegisterID
       WHERE prl.LineType IN ('Regular Earnings', 'Overtime Earnings')
       GROUP BY pr.PayrollPeriodID
   )
   SELECT COUNT(*) AS Periods,
       SUM(CASE WHEN ABS(c.Hours - r.Hours) > 0.001
           OR ABS(r.Hours - p.Hours) > 0.001 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           AS PeriodsThatDiffer,
       ROUND(SUM(c.Hours), 1) AS Clocked,
       ROUND(SUM(r.Hours), 1) AS Recorded,
       ROUND(SUM(p.Hours), 1) AS Paid
   FROM Clocked AS c
       INNER JOIN Recorded AS r ON r.PayrollPeriodID = c.PayrollPeriodID
       INNER JOIN Paid AS p ON p.PayrollPeriodID = c.PayrollPeriodID;
   ```

b. Read PeriodsThatDiffer and the three totals.

The three records agree in every pay period: the hours clocked are the hours recorded and the hours paid. Step 4 tests whether each paid hour belongs to the employee who was paid.

**Step 3. Look at the months with little indirect time.** Splitting the manufacturing hours of each pay period of fiscal 2024 by kind of labor shows what the records hold for those months.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H3: the manufacturing hours of 2024 by kind
   -- Population: manufacturing labor time; expected: every period recorded
   SELECT pp.PeriodNumber, pp.PeriodStartDate,
       ROUND(SUM(lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours), 0) AS Hours,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE lt.LaborType WHEN 'Direct Manufacturing'
           THEN lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END), 0)
           AS DirectHours,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE lt.LaborType WHEN 'Indirect Manufacturing'
           THEN lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END), 0)
           AS IndirectHours
   FROM LaborTimeEntry AS lt
       INNER JOIN PayrollPeriod AS pp
           ON pp.PayrollPeriodID = lt.PayrollPeriodID
   WHERE lt.LaborType <> 'NonManufacturing' AND pp.FiscalYear = 2024
   GROUP BY pp.PayrollPeriodID, pp.PeriodNumber, pp.PeriodStartDate
   ORDER BY pp.PeriodStartDate;
   ```

b. Read the IndirectHours of the periods from February to May.

The result answers the second question that Chapter 11 handed on. From February to May 2024, the plant recorded normal hours in every pay period, and most of them were direct time; from June, a large part of most periods is indirect. Nothing is missing from those months. The plant was building stock: in its first months it completed thousands of units more than it shipped, which kept most hours on work orders. When production fell back to the rate of shipments in the summer, the same employees kept their hours, and the time that no work order needed became indirect time. Exercise 12.3 measures the build.

**Step 4. Test whose time was paid.** A payroll earnings line points to the labor time entry it pays, so each line can be checked against the employee paid and against the approval of the clock entry behind it. Employee appears twice in the test, as pe for the employee paid and as we for the employee who worked, so that each row can show both.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H4: time paid to another person or unapproved
   -- Population: all earnings lines; expected: no rows
   SELECT 'Time paid to another employee' AS Test,
       pr.EmployeeID AS PaidID, pe.JobTitle AS PaidTitle,
       lt.EmployeeID AS WorkedID, we.JobTitle AS WorkedTitle,
       we.TerminationDate AS WorkerLeft, prl.Amount
   FROM PayrollRegisterLine AS prl
       INNER JOIN PayrollRegister AS pr
           ON pr.PayrollRegisterID = prl.PayrollRegisterID
       INNER JOIN LaborTimeEntry AS lt
           ON lt.LaborTimeEntryID = prl.LaborTimeEntryID
       INNER JOIN Employee AS pe ON pe.EmployeeID = pr.EmployeeID
       INNER JOIN Employee AS we ON we.EmployeeID = lt.EmployeeID
   WHERE lt.EmployeeID <> pr.EmployeeID
   UNION ALL
   SELECT 'Time paid on an unapproved clock entry',
       pr.EmployeeID, pe.JobTitle, lt.EmployeeID, we.JobTitle,
       we.TerminationDate, prl.Amount
   FROM PayrollRegisterLine AS prl
       INNER JOIN PayrollRegister AS pr
           ON pr.PayrollRegisterID = prl.PayrollRegisterID
       INNER JOIN LaborTimeEntry AS lt
           ON lt.LaborTimeEntryID = prl.LaborTimeEntryID
       INNER JOIN Employee AS pe ON pe.EmployeeID = pr.EmployeeID
       INNER JOIN Employee AS we ON we.EmployeeID = lt.EmployeeID
       INNER JOIN TimeClockEntry AS tc
           ON tc.TimeClockEntryID = lt.TimeClockEntryID
   WHERE tc.ClockStatus <> 'Approved';
   ```

b. Compare the PaidID and WorkedID of each row, and read the job titles.

The first test finds six earnings lines that pay one employee's time to others. The time belongs to an Inventory Specialist who left in September 2024, and the lines pay it to two other employees, another Inventory Specialist and an Assembler on the manufacturing payroll. The second test finds eight lines paid on clock entries not yet approved, two of them the Assembler's own time, and four of them lines that fail the first test as well. The amounts are small, but the exceptions reach the manufacturing payroll, and each needs a disposition.

**Step 5. Compare the pay with an expectation.** A reconciliation compares two records; an expectation compares a record with what other data imply. Each earnings line should equal its hours times the employee's base hourly rate from the Employee table, and time and a half for overtime. Set the threshold before you run the test: a line that differs by more than one cent, the rounding of one amount, is an exception.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H5: earnings paid against hours and pay rates
   -- Population: hourly earnings lines; expected: within a cent a line
   WITH Expected AS (
       SELECT pp.FiscalYear, prl.Amount,
           prl.Hours * e.BaseHourlyRate
               * CASE prl.LineType WHEN 'Overtime Earnings'
                   THEN 1.5 ELSE 1 END AS ExpectedAmount
       FROM PayrollRegisterLine AS prl
           INNER JOIN PayrollRegister AS pr
               ON pr.PayrollRegisterID = prl.PayrollRegisterID
           INNER JOIN PayrollPeriod AS pp
               ON pp.PayrollPeriodID = pr.PayrollPeriodID
           INNER JOIN Employee AS e ON e.EmployeeID = pr.EmployeeID
       WHERE prl.LineType IN ('Regular Earnings', 'Overtime Earnings')
   )
   SELECT FiscalYear, ROUND(SUM(Amount), 2) AS EarningsPaid,
       ROUND(SUM(ExpectedAmount), 2) AS Expected,
       ROUND(SUM(Amount) - SUM(ExpectedAmount), 2) AS Difference,
       SUM(CASE WHEN ABS(Amount - ExpectedAmount) > 0.01 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           AS LinesAboveOneCent
   FROM Expected
   GROUP BY FiscalYear
   ORDER BY FiscalYear;
   ```

b. Read the Difference and LinesAboveOneCent columns.

The earnings paid differ from the expectation by a few dollars a year, the sum of each line's rounding, and no line differs by more than a cent. Every hour was paid at the employee's rate, and every overtime hour at time and a half. The pay is right for the hours, so the rest of the tutorial asks about the hours themselves.

**Step 6. Test overtime against its approvals.** A time clock entry with overtime links to an overtime approval, and classifying the entries by the length of their overtime shows where the policy draws the line.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H6: overtime and its approvals
   -- Population: clock entries with overtime; expected: approved
   SELECT
       CASE WHEN OvertimeHours <= 0.5 THEN 'Half an hour or less'
           ELSE 'More than half an hour' END AS OvertimeLength,
       COUNT(*) AS Entries,
       SUM(CASE WHEN OvertimeApprovalID IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           AS WithoutApproval,
       ROUND(SUM(OvertimeHours), 1) AS OvertimeHours
   FROM TimeClockEntry
   WHERE OvertimeHours > 0
   GROUP BY OvertimeLength;
   ```

b. Compare the WithoutApproval column of the two rows.
c. Type and run the test below, which lists the longer entries without an approval and looks for an approval of the same employee and day. Employee appears twice again, as e for the employee and as ap for the approver.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H7: long overtime without an approval
   -- Population: overtime above half an hour; expected: no rows
   SELECT e.JobTitle, e.TerminationDate, tc.WorkDate,
       tc.OvertimeHours, tc.ClockOutTime, tc.ClockStatus,
       oa.OvertimeApprovalID AS UnlinkedApproval,
       ap.JobTitle AS ApprovedBy
   FROM TimeClockEntry AS tc
       INNER JOIN Employee AS e ON e.EmployeeID = tc.EmployeeID
       LEFT JOIN OvertimeApproval AS oa
           ON oa.EmployeeID = tc.EmployeeID AND oa.WorkDate = tc.WorkDate
       LEFT JOIN Employee AS ap ON ap.EmployeeID = oa.ApprovedByEmployeeID
   WHERE tc.OvertimeHours > 0.5 AND tc.OvertimeApprovalID IS NULL;
   ```

No entry with half an hour of overtime or less has an approval, while nearly every longer one does, which suggests a policy that exempts short overtime; the team should confirm it with the payroll department rather than assume it. Above that threshold, only three entries lack an approval link, all for the Inventory Specialist of Step 4, on New Year's Day of each year, still Pending, with no clock-out time, and two of them after the employee left. The left join finds an approval for each, entered by the Warehouse Manager, but none is linked to its entry.

**Step 7. Look for days on which everyone clocked the same hours.** Employees who clock in and out themselves arrive and leave at slightly different times, so a day on which every hourly employee of a plant recorded exactly the same hours is unusual; this chapter calls such a day a surge day. The CTE PlantDays counts, for each day, the employees and the different numbers of hours they recorded, and the final query summarizes the surge days by year.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H8: days when everyone clocked the same hours
   -- Population: manufacturing clock entries; expected: no such days
   WITH PlantDays AS (
       SELECT tc.WorkDate, COUNT(*) AS Employees,
           COUNT(DISTINCT tc.RegularHours + tc.OvertimeHours)
               AS HourPatterns,
           SUM(tc.OvertimeHours) AS OvertimeHours
       FROM TimeClockEntry AS tc
           INNER JOIN Employee AS e ON e.EmployeeID = tc.EmployeeID
           INNER JOIN CostCenter AS cc ON cc.CostCenterID = e.CostCenterID
       WHERE cc.CostCenterName = 'Manufacturing'
       GROUP BY tc.WorkDate
   )
   SELECT strftime('%Y', WorkDate) AS WorkYear,
       SUM(CASE WHEN HourPatterns = 1 AND Employees > 1
           THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS SurgeDays,
       MAX(CASE WHEN HourPatterns = 1 AND Employees > 1
           THEN Employees END) AS EmployeesPerDay,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN HourPatterns = 1 AND Employees > 1
           THEN OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END), 0) AS SurgeOvertime,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN HourPatterns = 1 AND Employees > 1
           THEN OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END) / SUM(OvertimeHours), 3)
           AS SurgeShare
   FROM PlantDays
   GROUP BY WorkYear
   ORDER BY WorkYear;
   ```

b. Read SurgeDays and SurgeShare for each year.

The result, shown in @fig-12-08, is the most important finding of the audit. On a growing number of days since mid-2024, all 64 hourly manufacturing employees recorded the same hours. @fig-12-09 shows six of them on such a day and on an ordinary day before the first one. On the surge day, they worked eight regular hours and four and a half of overtime, clocked in and out at the same minutes on one of two shifts, and the Production Manager approved all of the overtime on the work date. The overtime of the surge days grew to more than two-thirds of the plant's overtime by fiscal 2026, while overtime on other days, which Exercise 12.4 compares, stayed about the same. Identical times for a whole plant look like time entered in bulk rather than clocked by each employee. They do not prove that the hours were not worked, but the records cannot show that they were.

![Days on Which Every Hourly Manufacturing Employee Clocked the Same Hours.](/visuals/svg/fig-12-08-surge-days.svg){#fig-12-08 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL editor and its result. The editor, on the tab Audit.sql, shows a test that groups the manufacturing time clock entries by day in a CTE, counts the different numbers of hours recorded each day, and summarizes by year the days on which every employee recorded the same hours. The result has one row for each of 2024, 2025, and 2026, with the number of such days, which rises each year, the 64 employees on each of them, their overtime hours, and their share of the year's manufacturing overtime, which rises from about a third to more than two-thirds. The SurgeDays and SurgeShare columns are outlined."}

![A Day Before the Surge Days and a Surge Day.](/visuals/svg/fig-12-09-normal-and-surge-day.svg){#fig-12-09 fig-alt="Two tables of the time clock entries of the same six Assemblers. On a day in March 2024, before the first surge day, their clock-in and clock-out times differ by minutes and hours, their regular hours vary, and only some of them worked overtime, approved by the Production Manager. On a surge day in June 2026, all six clocked in and out at the same minutes on one of two shifts and recorded the same regular and overtime hours, all approved by the Production Manager on the work date; those cells are highlighted. A line under each table summarizes the day for all 64 hourly manufacturing employees: many different clock-in times and numbers of hours on the first day, and two clock-in times and one number of hours on the surge day, when every employee worked overtime."}

**Step 8. Test when direct labor was recorded.** Direct labor is recorded against a work order operation, which has an actual end date, and time recorded after that date was charged to work that was already finished. A CTE lists the surge days again, and a left join marks the time recorded on them.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H9: direct time recorded after its operation
   -- Population: direct labor time; expected: a small share
   WITH SurgeDays AS (
       SELECT tc.WorkDate
       FROM TimeClockEntry AS tc
           INNER JOIN Employee AS e ON e.EmployeeID = tc.EmployeeID
           INNER JOIN CostCenter AS cc ON cc.CostCenterID = e.CostCenterID
       WHERE cc.CostCenterName = 'Manufacturing'
       GROUP BY tc.WorkDate
       HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT tc.RegularHours + tc.OvertimeHours) = 1
           AND COUNT(*) > 1
   )
   SELECT strftime('%Y', lt.WorkDate) AS WorkYear,
       ROUND(SUM(lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours), 0) AS DirectHours,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN lt.WorkDate > op.ActualEndDate
           THEN lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END), 0)
           AS AfterEnd,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN lt.WorkDate > op.ActualEndDate
           THEN lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
           / SUM(lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours), 3) AS ShareAfterEnd,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN lt.WorkDate > op.ActualEndDate
           AND sd.WorkDate IS NOT NULL
           THEN lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END), 0)
           AS AfterEndOnSurgeDays
   FROM LaborTimeEntry AS lt
       INNER JOIN WorkOrderOperation AS op
           ON op.WorkOrderOperationID = lt.WorkOrderOperationID
       LEFT JOIN SurgeDays AS sd ON sd.WorkDate = lt.WorkDate
   WHERE lt.LaborType = 'Direct Manufacturing'
   GROUP BY WorkYear
   ORDER BY WorkYear;
   ```

b. Read ShareAfterEnd and AfterEndOnSurgeDays for each year.

The result, shown in @fig-12-10, rises from about a fifth of direct labor in fiscal 2024 to half in fiscal 2025 and about two-thirds in fiscal 2026, and most of the late time was recorded on surge days. Exercise 12.3 finds the month in which the share first jumped. The inner join leaves out the few direct entries with no valid operation that Tutorial 10.3 found.

![Direct Labor Recorded After Its Operation Ended.](/visuals/svg/fig-12-10-labor-after-operation-end.svg){#fig-12-10 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL editor and its result. The editor, on the tab Audit.sql, is scrolled past a CTE of surge days to a query that joins direct labor time entries to their work order operations, compares each work date with the operation's actual end date, and left-joins the surge days. The result has one row for each year, with the direct hours, the hours recorded after the operation had ended, their share, which rises from about a fifth in 2024 to about half in 2025 and about two-thirds in 2026, and the part of them recorded on surge days, which is most of them. The share and surge-day columns are outlined."}

**Step 9. Find where the late time was charged.** Splitting the direct time of fiscal 2026 by work center shows which operations received the time recorded after they had ended.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.3, test H10: late direct time by work center, 2026
   -- Population: direct labor time of 2026; expected: a small share
   SELECT wc.WorkCenterName,
       ROUND(SUM(lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours), 0) AS DirectHours,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN lt.WorkDate > op.ActualEndDate
           THEN lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours ELSE 0 END)
           / SUM(lt.RegularHours + lt.OvertimeHours), 3) AS ShareAfterEnd
   FROM LaborTimeEntry AS lt
       INNER JOIN WorkOrderOperation AS op
           ON op.WorkOrderOperationID = lt.WorkOrderOperationID
       INNER JOIN WorkCenter AS wc ON wc.WorkCenterID = op.WorkCenterID
   WHERE lt.LaborType = 'Direct Manufacturing'
       AND lt.WorkDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
   GROUP BY wc.WorkCenterID, wc.WorkCenterName
   ORDER BY ShareAfterEnd DESC;
   ```

b. Compare the ShareAfterEnd of the work centers.

At Packing, the last operation of every routing, nearly all the direct time of fiscal 2026 was recorded after the operation had ended, and at Quality Assurance most of it was. The hours above plan at those work centers in Tutorial 11.2 are time charged to operations already complete, so the operation records cannot say which operations the direct time belongs to.

**Step 10. Complete and save the script.** The header comment should record the checks that the chapter's tests passed.

a. Replace the last line of the header comment of Audit.sql, so that the header reads as below.

   ```sql
   /* Audit.sql: tests of the records behind the manufacturing variance
      Database: CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite (a copy of CharlesRiver.sqlite)
      Prepared by: your name, date; reviewed by: name, date
      Checks: populations tie to the ledger; exceptions listed by test */
   ```

b. Click **Save SQL file**.

The script now holds every test of the chapter under a comment that names it and states its population and expected result, the structure of the audit query library in @tbl-12-01.

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- the profile finds a handful of entries awaiting approval and three with no clock-out time, in records that end on 11 December 2026;
- clocked, recorded, and paid hours agree in every pay period, and the manufacturing hours of February to May 2024 are complete, most of them direct;
- six earnings lines pay a terminated employee's time to others, two of them to an Assembler, and eight rest on unapproved clock entries;
- every earnings line agrees with the expectation from its hours and the employee's rate to within a cent;
- long overtime is approved, except three entries of the terminated employee whose approvals are not linked;
- on a growing number of days every hourly manufacturing employee clocked the same hours, and by fiscal 2026 those days carried more than two-thirds of the plant's overtime;
- the share of direct time recorded after its operation ended rose to about two-thirds, most of it on surge days and at Packing;
- Audit.sql is saved with a completed header and a comment above each test.

The tests support part of the controller's explanation. The hours behind the variance were recorded, paid at the right rates, and posted, and the manufacturing payroll ties to the ledger, so the variance is a cost that the plant's records say it incurred. The growth in overtime, though, sits on surge days whose identical times, single approver, and charges to finished operations the records cannot explain. The chief audit executive will report the exceptions for correction, the time-recording practice as a weakness in the design of controls, and the surge-day overtime as a matter to corroborate before the committee relies on it.
